subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In close reading, attending to 'syntax' means examining:
options: the historical period of the text
the rhyme scheme of a stanza
the choice of individual words for connotation
the arrangement and ordering of words into sentence structures and their effects
questions.explain: Syntax concerns sentence structure and word order, whose patterning shapes pace, emphasis and meaning.

questions.q: In Tess of the d'Urbervilles, the protagonist's destruction by social judgement, chance and inflexible circumstance most closely fits the model of:
options: modern/social tragedy in which an essentially blameless figure is crushed by hostile forces
comic tragedy with a restorative ending
the wholly culpable tragic villain
classical tragedy with a formal chorus
questions.explain: Tess exemplifies a modern tragedy of victimhood, undone by social cruelty and circumstance more than personal fault.

questions.q: Aristotle valued a 'complex' plot over a 'simple' one because the complex plot includes:
options: more characters
a longer chorus
a happy ending
both peripeteia and anagnorisis, producing a stronger tragic effect
questions.explain: For Aristotle the finest tragic plots combine reversal and recognition, intensifying pity and fear.

questions.q: A 'tragic victim' differs from a 'tragic hero' principally in that the victim:
options: is responsible for the catastrophe alone
suffers ruin largely through forces or others' actions beyond their control rather than through their own decisive error
always survives the play
causes the downfall of everyone else
questions.explain: The tragic victim is destroyed more by external forces or circumstance than by a self-generated fatal error.

questions.q: 'Dramatic irony' occurs when:
options: the audience knows something a character on stage does not
a character speaks in verse while others speak in prose
the play breaks the fourth wall
the chorus comments on the action
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises from the gap between the audience's knowledge and a character's ignorance of it.

questions.q: Which sentence best demonstrates an integrated, analytical (rather than descriptive) point?
options: The character is angry in this scene.
This passage is about anger and conflict.
Anger is a theme that appears in the text.
The clipped monosyllables and end-stopped lines enact the speaker's controlled rage, refusing the release that fuller rhythm would allow.
questions.explain: Analytical writing links a precise technique to its effect on meaning, rather than merely naming a theme.

questions.q: 'Framing' as a structural device most often refers to:
options: the use of iambic pentameter throughout
the metaphors clustered in a single stanza
the alphabetical ordering of chapters
a story enclosed within another narrative that introduces and concludes it
questions.explain: A frame narrative encloses an inner tale, often shaping how the reader judges its reliability and meaning.

questions.q: Shakespearean tragedy typically departs from strict classical models by:
options: observing the three unities rigidly
mingling subplots, comic elements and a broad sweep of time and place
avoiding any soliloquy
always employing a formal chorus
questions.explain: Shakespeare loosens the classical unities, weaving subplots, comedy and expansive action into the tragic structure.

questions.q: In a play like Othello, the figure who engineers the hero's destruction through manipulation exemplifies the convention of:
options: the tragic villain whose scheming exploits the hero's vulnerability
the deus ex machina
the tragic chorus
the comic servant
questions.explain: The tragic villain actively engineers catastrophe, exploiting the hero's weaknesses to bring about the fall.

questions.q: A response arguing that a text 'cannot be reduced to a single meaning' and surveying competing readings is engaging most strongly with:
options: AO4
AO1 only
AO5
AO2 only
questions.explain: Acknowledging multiple, competing interpretations is the core of AO5.

questions.q: The 'tragic arc' of a conventional tragedy moves broadly:
options: from comedy to romance
in a circle returning to the start unchanged
from suffering to restored happiness
from a position of stature, through error and reversal, to catastrophe and often recognition
questions.explain: The tragic arc descends from elevation through hamartia and peripeteia to catastrophe, often by way of anagnorisis.

questions.q: A 'reader-response' approach holds that meaning is:
options: fixed entirely by the author's stated intention
irrelevant to literary study
produced in the interaction between the text and the reader's act of interpretation
determined solely by the historical context of composition
questions.explain: Reader-response criticism locates meaning in the transaction between text and reader rather than in the author alone.

questions.q: An 'unreliable narrator' is one whose:
options: narration is consistently omniscient and authoritative
perspective shifts between several characters
story is told entirely in the present tense
account the reader is invited to question because their credibility is compromised
questions.explain: An unreliable narrator's version of events is undermined by gaps, bias or self-deception that the reader must read against.

questions.q: An 'ecocritical' reading would be most interested in:
options: the relationship between the text, the non-human world and the environment
the repressed desires of the central characters
the gendered power relations within the household
the text's depiction of class struggle
questions.explain: Ecocriticism examines how literature represents nature, place and humanity's relationship with the environment.

questions.q: 'Catharsis' is frequently debated by critics because:
options: Aristotle defined it at exhaustive length
Aristotle left the term under-explained, prompting rival readings as purgation, purification or clarification
it appears only in modern drama
it refers solely to the hero's death
questions.explain: The brevity of Aristotle's account has generated competing interpretations of what catharsis actually achieves.

questions.q: 'Nemesis' in the tragic pattern refers to:
options: the comic foil to the protagonist
the hero's initial good fortune
the prologue of the play
the agent or process of retribution that brings the hero's downfall
questions.explain: Nemesis is the retributive force or fate that punishes the hero's transgression, completing the tragic arc.

questions.q: At A-level, AO1 chiefly assesses a candidate's ability to:
options: explore how different readers interpret a text
articulate an informed, personal response using a coherent, accurate critical argument and terminology
analyse the influence of contexts on a text
analyse the writer's use of form, structure and language
questions.explain: AO1 rewards a coherent, well-written argument expressed in accurate critical terminology with relevant textual support.

questions.q: In tragedy, 'hubris' refers to:
options: the audience's pity
the hero's humility before the gods
the chorus's lament
excessive pride or overreaching that affronts the moral or divine order
questions.explain: Hubris is overweening pride or presumption that violates limits and invites the hero's downfall.

questions.q: The most sophisticated use of a critical quotation is to:
options: agree with it uncritically
place it at the end as a flourish
ignore it entirely
engage with it dialectically, qualifying or contesting it through close textual evidence
questions.explain: AO5 rewards a critical dialogue with other readings, tested against the student's own analysis of the text.

questions.q: The tragic emotion of 'pity' in Aristotle's scheme is typically aroused by:
options: the hero's complete villainy
the comic subplot
undeserved misfortune befalling someone like ourselves
the restoration of order
questions.explain: Pity, for Aristotle, responds to undeserved suffering, while fear arises from recognising the hero as like ourselves.

questions.q: The 'fatal flaw' in a tragic hero is most precisely a trait that:
options: belongs only to the villain
has no bearing on the plot
makes the hero comic
is admirable in itself yet becomes destructive under pressure, driving the catastrophe
questions.explain: The fatal flaw is often a virtue carried to excess, which, under pressure, precipitates the hero's ruin.

questions.q: A response that explores how a text can sustain feminist, Marxist and psychoanalytic readings is primarily demonstrating which assessment objective?
options: AO3
AO5
AO2
AO4
questions.explain: AO5 rewards engagement with different interpretations, including the application of distinct critical lenses.

questions.q: In Aristotle's Poetics, 'hamartia' is best understood as:
options: the tragic hero's error of judgement or flaw that precipitates their downfall
the audience's emotional purging at the play's close
the moment of fatal recognition
the reversal of fortune from good to bad
questions.explain: Hamartia is the tragic hero's mistake or flaw, the error from which the catastrophe ultimately flows.

questions.q: A 'post-colonial' reading is most concerned with:
options: metre and rhyme scheme
representations of empire, the colonised 'other', hybridity and cultural power
the purging of pity and fear in the audience
the recurrence of a single image
questions.explain: Post-colonial criticism interrogates how texts construct empire, the colonised subject and relations of cultural power.

questions.q: Which is the best example of using context (AO3) analytically rather than as 'bolted-on' background?
options: A paragraph narrating the author's biography before discussing the text
Showing how the poem's anxieties about industrialisation shape its imagery of the polluted river
Stating that the text was written in the nineteenth century
Listing the dates of the period at the essay's start
questions.explain: Context is used well when it illuminates specific textual choices rather than sitting as detached background.

questions.q: A.C. Bradley's influential approach to Shakespearean tragedy is associated with close attention to:
options: the printing history of the quartos
stage machinery
the psychology and 'character' of the tragic hero
the costumes of the players
questions.explain: Bradley's criticism foregrounds the tragic hero's character and inner psychology as the engine of the tragedy.

questions.q: 'Tone' in a literary text refers to:
options: the writer's or speaker's attitude towards the subject, conveyed through diction and form
the literal sound of words read aloud
the historical setting
the moral lesson of the work
questions.explain: Tone is the implied attitude or stance of the speaker towards subject or audience, signalled by linguistic choices.

questions.q: The convention of the 'tragic waste' refers to:
options: the chorus's idleness
the comic subplot's failure
the destruction of much that is valuable, leaving a sense of loss beyond the hero alone
the absence of any deaths
questions.explain: Tragic waste names the loss of admirable lives and potential, deepening the catastrophe's emotional weight.

questions.q: In narrative theory, 'free indirect discourse' is best defined as:
options: direct speech reported within quotation marks
an authorial commentary that judges the characters explicitly
a first-person narrator addressing the reader directly
a character's thoughts rendered in the third person yet inflected with that character's own idiom and feeling
questions.explain: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's third-person report with a character's voice, blurring the line between the two.

questions.q: The Aristotelian 'tragic hero' is conventionally a figure who is:
options: entirely passive and faultless
of high estate and essentially noble, whose downfall arises from error rather than mere vice
wholly villainous and deserving of punishment
comic in temperament
questions.explain: The classical tragic hero is elevated and largely virtuous, falling through hamartia rather than outright wickedness.
